units.title: Unit 27 — Sport
learningObjectives: Describe physical training, fitness and new sporting experiences using natural collocations.
Interpret sporting commentary about results, performances, referee decisions and scores.
Distinguish conversational sporting idioms from more neutral competition vocabulary.

items.example: Our training programme includes two recovery sessions each week.
items.note: A training programme is a structured sequence of physical preparation activities.

items.example: The national squad attended a training camp before the championship.
items.note: A training camp brings athletes together for intensive preparation over a period.

items.example: Some visitors do extreme sports while others prefer gentle walks.
items.note: Use do, rather than make, with the general category extreme sports.

items.example: White-water rafting requires careful attention to the instructor's signals.
items.note: White-water rafting involves navigating fast-flowing rivers in an inflatable raft.

items.example: Rock climbing taught Elena how to plan each movement carefully.
items.note: Rock climbing names a sport that involves ascending natural rock formations or walls.

items.example: After several lessons, I began to acquire a taste for indoor climbing.
items.note: Acquire a taste for describes gradually developing enjoyment of something unfamiliar.

items.example: Bend your knees slightly to keep your balance on the board.
items.note: Keep your balance is used for remaining physically steady while moving or standing.

items.example: It took me three attempts to get the hang of it, but then the movement felt natural.
items.note: Informal: get the hang of something means become able to do it through practice.

items.example: The younger players decided to take up the challenge despite their lack of experience.
items.note: Take up the challenge means accept a demanding opportunity or task.

items.example: Even though she is pretty fit, the long hike left her exhausted.
items.note: In informal English, pretty can mean fairly or quite; it does not refer to attractiveness here.

items.example: You should not push yourself to the limits without adequate recovery time.
items.note: This idiom means making an exceptionally great physical or mental effort.

items.example: After the overnight journey, he fell into a deep sleep almost immediately.
items.note: Fall into a deep sleep describes the transition to very sound sleep.

items.word: have a whale of a time
items.example: The volunteers had a whale of a time at the charity tournament.
items.note: Informal expression for enjoying an experience enormously.

items.example: I would jump at the chance to train with an Olympic athlete.
items.note: Jump at the chance means accept a desirable opportunity eagerly.

items.example: She had to summon up the energy for one last rehearsal.
items.note: Summon up the energy means deliberately find enough strength or motivation to act.

items.example: He cycles to work to keep in shape during the winter.
items.note: Keep in shape means maintain physical fitness over time.

items.pt: atingir um nível máximo de excitação ou tensão
items.example: Anticipation reached fever pitch just before the final whistle.
items.note: Fever pitch describes an extremely high degree of excitement, tension or emotion.

items.example: The visiting side secured a convincing victory in the final round.
items.note: Secure a victory stresses achieving the win; convincing indicates clear superiority.

items.example: Both teams took the field as the stadium lights came on.
items.note: Take the field is a conventional sports expression for players entering play.

items.example: The underdogs put up a determined performance against the league leaders.
items.note: Put up a performance describes how a competitor performs in an event.

items.pt: defesa formidável ou muito difícil de superar
items.example: The attackers struggled to penetrate the visitors' formidable defence.
items.note: Formidable defence describes a defensive line that is exceptionally difficult to overcome.

items.example: A quick exchange of passes helped the forwards break through the defence.
items.note: Break through the defence describes getting past opposing players to create an attack.

items.example: An impressive tackle stopped the winger near the corner flag.
items.note: Impressive can describe a skilful or powerful tackle; tackle is an attempt to stop an opponent.

items.pt: receber a marcação de um pênalti a favor
items.example: The home side was awarded a penalty after a foul in the box.
items.note: Be awarded a penalty means the referee grants a penalty to a team or player.

items.example: The striker missed a penalty when his shot hit the crossbar.
items.note: Miss a penalty means fail to score from a penalty kick, not fail to notice it.

items.example: The presenter reads the latest scores between news bulletins.
items.note: Latest scores refers to the most recently available match results or score updates.

items.example: At half-time, the score stands at two goals to one.
items.note: The score stands at introduces the current numerical result in sports reporting.

items.example: A reckless challenge earned the defender a yellow card.
items.note: A yellow card is an official caution in association football and several other sports.

items.example: The captain curled a free kick over the defensive wall.
items.note: A free kick restarts play after certain infringements; take a free kick is also natural.

items.example: A misplaced clearance caused the defender to score an own goal.
items.note: Score an own goal means accidentally put the ball into your own team's goal.

items.example: The crowd went wild when the substitute scored in extra time.
items.note: Go wild expresses an intense emotional reaction, often excitement but sometimes anger.

items.example: Extreme sports attract participants who enjoy controlled risks.
items.note: Extreme is the conventional adjective for potentially high-risk adventurous sports.

items.pt: manter a forma durante o inverno
items.example: Daily walks help me keep in shape over winter without paying for a gym.
items.note: Keep in shape remains natural when a time period specifies the fitness routine.

items.example: The news site displays the latest football scores on its front page.
items.note: Latest modifies scores; a sport name may specify which results are being reported.

items.example: The referee decided to award a penalty for deliberate handball.
items.note: Award a penalty is the active form with the referee as the grammatical subject.

items.example: The rookie put up an excellent performance in her first international race.
items.note: Put up an excellent performance focuses on the quality of someone's effort.

units.title: Unit 28 — Plans and decisions
learningObjectives: Present tentative proposals and identify the factors behind decisions with appropriate combinations.
Discuss planning, schedules, implementation and contingencies in professional contexts.
Use natural phrases for rejecting ideas, giving constructive criticism and reaching conclusions.

items.example: The research group is toying with an idea for a public exhibition.
items.note: Toy with an idea suggests considering it tentatively rather than deciding firmly.

items.example: Repairing the foundation is a long-term solution to the recurring leaks.
items.note: Long-term solution aims to deal with a problem sustainably, not just temporarily.

items.example: The director will unveil a plan for reducing energy consumption next week.
items.note: Unveil a plan means reveal or announce it for the first time.

items.example: Volunteers visited local schools to drum up support for the campaign.
items.note: Drum up support means actively generate enthusiasm or backing for an initiative.

items.example: A slight change of plan means the meeting will take place online.
items.note: Slight softens the size of a change; change of plan is a common fixed combination.

items.pt: seguir uma sugestão e agir com base nela
items.example: The committee agreed to act on a suggestion from the safety officer.
items.note: Act on means take concrete action because of advice or a proposal.

items.example: The agency will implement a plan to improve rural internet access.
items.note: Implement a plan means put a previously designed course of action into operation.

items.example: The coordinator asked us to draw up a schedule for the next three months.
items.note: Draw up is commonly used with formal documents, plans and timetables.

items.example: We can finish by Friday if everyone sticks to the agreed schedule.
items.note: Stick to means continue following a timetable despite distractions or obstacles.

items.example: May I make a tentative suggestion about the order of the presentations?
items.note: Tentative indicates that the proposal is provisional and open to discussion.

items.example: The council plans to launch a scheme that subsidises bicycle repairs.
items.note: Launch a scheme means formally begin an organised initiative or programme.

items.example: The charity wants to exercise greater control over how donations are spent.
items.note: Exercise control is a formal collocation meaning use authority to influence decisions.

items.pt: deixar a decisão a critério deles
items.example: We will leave it to their discretion whether the interview is recorded.
items.note: Leave something to someone's discretion delegates judgement or choice to that person.

items.example: The organisers prepared backup equipment to cover every eventuality.
items.note: Cover every eventuality means make preparations for all foreseeable possibilities.

items.example: The board will reach a decision after examining both proposals.
items.note: Reach a decision focuses on arriving at a choice after consideration.

items.example: After careful consideration, we decided to postpone the exhibition.
items.note: Formal phrase signalling that the choice follows deliberate thought.

items.example: With the road closed, the only option open to us was the ferry.
items.note: An option open to someone is a possible course of action available to them.

items.example: Accessibility was the deciding factor when we selected the venue.
items.note: The deciding factor is the consideration that ultimately determines the choice.

items.example: When the supplier cancelled, we had no choice but to seek a replacement.
items.note: Have no choice stresses that no viable alternative is available.

items.example: The students waited with eager anticipation for the competition results.
items.note: Eager anticipation combines excitement with expectation of a future event.

items.example: One of the interns came up with an idea for a more accessible website.
items.note: Come up with an idea means think of or propose a new idea.

items.example: Preparations are underway for the city's annual science festival.
items.note: Underway means currently happening; preparations are underway is an established phrase.

items.example: The legal team completed the necessary groundwork before negotiations began.
items.note: Groundwork is foundational work that makes a later undertaking possible.

items.example: The school found funding to put an idea into practice next term.
items.note: Put an idea into practice means transform a proposal into concrete action.

items.example: Once the budget was approved, we could turn our attention to recruitment.
items.note: Turn your attention to means shift your focus to a different matter.

items.example: Several residents declared outright opposition to the proposed motorway.
items.note: Outright strengthens opposition to indicate complete or unequivocal disagreement.

items.example: The proposal was met with outright hostility from several committee members.
items.note: Outright hostility implies a strong, unqualified negative reaction.

items.example: The manager rejected the revised proposal out of hand.
items.note: Reject out of hand means dismiss without serious consideration.

items.example: The team welcomed constructive criticism during the design review.
items.note: Constructive criticism identifies shortcomings with the intention of improvement.

items.example: The investigators came to a conclusion after reviewing the evidence.
items.note: Come to a conclusion is idiomatic; make a conclusion is not the normal form.

items.example: It is too early to arrive at a conclusion about the pilot's success.
items.note: Arrive at a conclusion is a slightly formal alternative to come to a conclusion.

items.example: A small grant helped the engineers make their prototype a reality.
items.note: Make something a reality means bring an intended or imagined result into existence.

items.example: Local volunteers did the groundwork before the community centre opened.
items.note: Do the groundwork is a natural verb phrase for preparatory activities.

items.word: option is not open to us
items.pt: essa opção não está disponível para nós
items.example: An extension is not open to us under the terms of the contract.
items.note: An option is not open to someone when it is unavailable or impractical.

items.example: We must make a decision about the contractor before Monday.
items.note: Make a decision focuses on choosing; reach a decision highlights arriving at that choice.

items.example: Final preparations for the conference include testing the microphones.
items.note: Final preparations are the last tasks completed before an event or launch.

items.example: An unexpected delivery delay forced a change of plan.
items.note: Change of plan is more idiomatic here than change of planning.

items.pt: agir com base em um conselho
items.example: The technician acted on advice from the manufacturer's support team.
items.note: Act on commonly combines with advice, information or a suggestion.
